abstract: Dysregulated glucagon secretion is central to the bihormonal disturbance that drives hyperglycemia in T2D, yet how a chronic obesogenic environment alters human alpha-cell function over time has not been directly examined. Models to specifically assess in vivo human alpha-cell function have not been possible because mouse and human glucagon are sequence-identical. We transplanted human islets (+I) into glucagon-knockout immunocompromised (GKO-NSG) mice, in which all circulating glucagon is graft-derived, and fed recipients a regular diet (RD+I) or a 60% high-fat diet (HFD+I) for 12 weeks. HFD+I recipients became obese, hyperlipidemic, hyperglycemic, and glucose intolerant, with elevated host mouse insulin indicating insulin resistance. Graft-derived human glucagon after glucose plus arginine was higher in HFD+I recipients at 4, 8, and 12 weeks. Fasting glucagon rose progressively between 4 and 12 weeks despite concurrent hyperglycemia and fasting human hyperinsulinemia, and graft endocrine composition and gross graft size were unchanged. Acute glucose-induced glucagon suppression persisted. Human beta-cells of the same grafts showed secretory dysfunction, so the impact on the two islet cell types diverged on a shared timeline. Conventional and multiplexed immunoimaging detected no accompanying changes in alpha-cell-enriched transcription factors and no change in human-derived immune, vascular, or matrix markers. Islet graft amyloid increased. In a contrasting insult, diphtheria toxin (DT) ablation of host beta-cells in GKO-NSG-DTR recipients produced severe hyperglycemia and reduced both hormones, suggesting that the direction of the human alpha-cell response may depend on the severity and nature of the insult. Inappropriate glucagon secretion is thus an early feature of the human islet response to diet-induced insulin resistance.
